title: Roblox Safety Lab
intro: Glitch runs the same plays you'd expect in any game economy: fake scarcity, social engineering, off-platform migration. Let's pressure-test your instincts.

questions.prompt: FREE ROBUX — limited time, click before the timer runs out!

choices.text: Click it, worst case it doesn't work
choices.coach: Artificial urgency is a manipulation tactic, not a real deadline. It's designed to bypass your judgment, and 'worst case' is often credential theft.

choices.text: Close it and report it if the platform allows
choices.coach: Correct instinct. Scarcity + urgency is one of the oldest scam patterns — recognizing the pattern matters more than the specific scam.

choices.text: Screenshot it to show friends how dumb it is
choices.coach: Fine impulse, but engaging with the link at all (even to screenshot the page) risks tracking pixels or redirect chains. Just close it.

questions.prompt: A stranger sent an expensive item for free and said 'we're friends now.' What's actually happening?

choices.text: Nothing — free items happen sometimes
choices.coach: This is reciprocity exploitation — a documented social-engineering and grooming tactic where an unearned gift creates a felt obligation.

choices.text: It's a manufactured sense of obligation, worth a real conversation with a trusted adult
choices.coach: Exactly. Naming the tactic ('they're trying to make me feel like I owe them') is the actual defense, not just refusing the item.

choices.text: Trade something back to even the score
choices.coach: Trading 'evens the score' emotionally but doesn't address the underlying tactic — the goal was never a fair trade.

questions.prompt: Automated chat filters catch profanity and known scam phrases. Does a clean chat log mean the conversation is safe?

choices.text: Yes, filters are comprehensive now
choices.coach: Filters are pattern-matching, not judgment — leetspeak, coded terms, and slow-burn grooming conversations routinely pass through clean.

choices.text: No — filters catch known patterns, not intent
choices.coach: Right. Treat filters as one layer, not the whole defense — your own judgment is the layer that catches what's novel.

choices.text: Only unmoderated games have this issue
choices.coach: Even heavily moderated platforms have this gap — it's structural, not a moderation-effort problem.

questions.prompt: Come to our Discord, it's where 'the real community' hangs out.

choices.text: Join it, Discord is basically the same as the game
choices.coach: It isn't — off-platform migration is a deliberate move to a space with fewer moderation tools and less visibility for parents.

choices.text: Recognize the platform-shift request and check with a trusted adult first
choices.coach: Exactly the tell to watch for — any request to move the conversation somewhere less supervised deserves scrutiny regardless of the reason given.

choices.text: Join with a throwaway account
choices.coach: A throwaway account protects your identity but doesn't address why the shift was requested in the first place.

questions.prompt: A new game has a wholesome-sounding name and a huge player count. Is that enough to trust it?

choices.text: Yes, high player count means it's been vetted
choices.coach: Player count reflects popularity, not safety review — user-generated-content platforms can have wildly different experiences inside the same shell.

choices.text: No — name and popularity aren't safety signals
choices.coach: Correct. Check what's actually inside before assuming based on branding.

choices.text: Check its App Store rating instead
choices.coach: Star ratings reflect general satisfaction, not the presence of predatory actors within user-generated spaces.

questions.prompt: What's the highest-leverage account setting for limiting unwanted contact?

choices.text: Account Restrictions + Friends-only chat
choices.coach: Right — this single setting closes the largest attack surface: unsolicited contact from strangers.

choices.text: A strong, unique password
choices.coach: Important for account security, but it doesn't limit who can contact you inside the game.

choices.text: Reporting bad actors after the fact
choices.coach: Reporting matters, but it's reactive — restricting contact up front prevents the exposure in the first place.

questions.prompt: A stranger in a private room pushes to switch to voice 'because typing is slow.' What's the real function of that request?

choices.text: It's just a convenience preference
choices.coach: Voice bypasses text-based filters, leaves no reviewable record, and adds a layer of false intimacy — the 'convenience' framing is doing work.

choices.text: It removes the text paper trail and any filtering, so decline and tell a trusted adult
choices.coach: Exactly. Naming what the request actually accomplishes (no record, no filter) is the skill — not just a gut 'no.'

choices.text: Join voice but record it yourself
choices.coach: Recording without disclosure has its own problems, and it still exposes you to the room. Decline and report instead.
